rows: Broke, Baby Sick, and Car Trouble!

Dorothea Lange wrote down what people told her, and this family's own words became her title. Their car, loaded with belongings, broke down on a California highway as they searched for work during the Depression.
What would you do if your car broke down far from home?
The Hindenburg Disaster

On May 6, 1937, the German airship Hindenburg burst into flames as it landed in Lakehurst, New Jersey, killing 36 people. Photographers like Sam Shere were waiting for the landing, and these pictures ended the age of giant passenger airships.
Why do you think airships don't carry passengers today?
Hardware Store, Bowery, New York
Berenice Abbott photographed New York for years to record how fast it was changing. This hardware store spills pails, paints and tools onto the sidewalk and shows how a shop looked in the 1930s.
What tools do you recognize?
Open-Air Barber, Belzoni, Mississippi
A barber trims a customer's hair on a porch in a Mississippi town while other men wait. Marion Post Wolcott photographed daily life in the Deep South for the government.
Would you want a haircut outdoors?
Church, Pie Town, New Mexico

Pie Town got its name from a woman who baked pies for travelers. Russell Lee photographed its homesteader families in color in 1940, and the pictures give a vivid look at a farming community. Here people gather outside a log church.
What does the church building look like?
Working on a Vengeance Dive Bomber

During World War II, millions of women took jobs in factories. Alfred Palmer photographed women at the Vultee plant in Tennessee as they worked on a dive bomber. His color pictures were meant to show Americans pulling together.
What jobs do you think the women are doing?
Woman Machinist, Douglas Aircraft
A woman operates a drilling machine in a factory making airplanes during World War II. Women like her took jobs that men had left to go to war, and posters called them Rosie the Riveter.
What would you build if you worked in a factory?
Bethlehem Steel Mill, Sparrows Point
Smoking stacks and giant furnaces fill the sky at a steel mill in Maryland. John Vachon photographed American towns and factories for the Farm Security Administration.
What do you think steel was used for?
Michigan Avenue, Chicago
John Vachon photographed the tall buildings of Chicago's Michigan Avenue from a street corner. Chicago invented the skyscraper, and this street shows why people loved the city.
How many tall buildings can you count?
Children in Color
Marion Post Wolcott photographed children in the American South on color film. At a time when most photographs were black-and-white, her color pictures show warm clothing and sunlight.
What color do you notice first?
Schoolchildren, Pie Town, New Mexico
Four girls smile in a classroom in a small New Mexico town. Russell Lee photographed their one-room school and the children who came from farms for miles around.
What would it be like to go to a one-room school?
